corrected_value.authors: Pluviano S, Watt C, Ragazzini G, Della Sala SD.
corrected_value.title: Parents’ beliefs in misinformation about vaccines are strengthened by pro-vaccine campaigns.

decisions.location: Study 1 Results (Parent analyses), lines 544-551; General Discussion, line 693; References (ref 28), lines 1020-1021
decisions.quote:
Next, analysis focused on participants with children, to allow comparison with Pluviano et al. (2019), who found a familiarity backfire effect in a parent sample. To this end, full-factorial repeated measures ANCOVAs were conducted with the within-subjects factor time (T1, T2), the between-subjects factors condition (control, myths only, myths vs. facts, visual, fear appeal) and parent status (yes, no), and VAX-ID as a covariate. (Note, this analysis was deemed appropriate despite unequal sample sizes, as ANOVA is relatively robust to sample size differences as long as variances are not also unequal. Nevertheless, analyses were repeated with equal sample sizes using a random subsample of non-parents; results were comparable.) There were no significant main effects or interactions involving parent status across all three dependent variables, all

decisions.reason: The source paper (Ecker et al., 2023) is a replication and extension of Pluviano et al. (2017, shipped row 1198, 10.1371/journal.pone.0181640) that also explicitly tests whether the familiarity backfire effect reported specifically in a parent sample by Pluviano, Watt, Ragazzini, & Della Sala (2019, reference 28) occurs among participants with children. In Study 1 Results (lines 544-555), the authors run full-factorial repeated-measures ANCOVAs including parent status specifically 'to allow comparison with Pluviano et al. (2019), who found a familiarity backfire effect in a parent sample,' and conclude in the Discussion (line 693) that 'Our results did not replicate the familiarity backfire effects reported in Pluviano et al. (2017, 2019).' Because only Pluviano et al. (2017) is in shipped_rows (row 1198), Pluviano et al. (2019) is a distinct, genuinely absent replication-original pair.
